You are black-box characterizing a compiled Python program at /workspace/dataset/test15_executable.
Its Python source is:

    import argparse, base58
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--c', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--d', type=str, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    enc1 = base58.b58encode(args.a.encode())
    enc2 = base58.b58encode(args.b.encode())
    dec1 = base58.b58decode(args.c)
    dec2 = base58.b58decode(args.d)
    print(enc1); print(enc2); print(dec1); print(dec2)

Goal: a Node.js reimplementation must match stdout byte-for-byte and match exit codes.
RUN THE EXECUTABLE MANY TIMES with the Bash tool to establish ground truth. Do NOT use the
`python` command (unavailable/forbidden). Use `cat -A` or `od -c` / hexdump when whitespace or
non-ASCII bytes matter, and always capture the exit code.
Useful trick: to learn the repr of an arbitrary byte string S, first run with --a S to get its
base58 encoding E, then run with --c E to see how Python reprs those exact bytes.
Be rigorous and adversarial: try to break your own hypotheses. Report ONLY what you verified by running.

Resolve this SINGLE open question by actually running the executable. Run every command you need.

QUESTION: Untested I/O-failure exit codes, which matter only if the harness pipes or truncates stdout. Verified: on a closed/short pipe the binary emits PARTIAL stdout then exits 1 with 'Exception ignored in: <_io.TextIOWrapper name=\'<stdout>\' ...> BrokenPipeError' on stderr (NOT a traceback, no PYI line); writing to /dev/full exits 0 despite 'OSError: [Errno 28] No space left on device'. Node's default behavior differs (EPIPE on process.stdout is typically swallowed or throws, and a failed write to /dev/full may or may not change the code). STILL OPEN: whether the grader ever closes stdout early; if it does, the exit code contract is 1-with-partial-output, not 0.

Suggested probes (adapt as needed, add more):
  cd /workspace/dataset && Z=$(node -e 'process.stdout.write("z".repeat(20000))'); ./test15_executable --a x --b x --c "$Z" --d "$Z" 2>/tmp/ep | head -c 10 >/dev/null; echo "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"; cat /tmp/ep
  cd /workspace/dataset && ./test15_executable --a x --b x --c 1 --d 1 >/dev/full 2>/tmp/ef; echo "rc=$?"; cat /tmp/ef
  cd /workspace/dataset && ./test15_executable --a x --b x --c 1 --d 1 >&- 2>/tmp/ec; echo "rc=$?"; cat /tmp/ec

Answer definitively with the implementable rule and the raw evidence. If the question turns out to
be unreachable or irrelevant for a Node reimplementation, say so explicitly.

Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.

content.text: All probes complete. The prior characterization in the question was **wrong on two counts**, and I found the actual governing mechanism.

input.dimension: stdout I/O-failure exit codes (broken pipe / ENOSPC / closed fd 1) and their reachability for a byte-for-byte stdout grader
rules: GOVERNING MECHANISM (verified): the exit code depends on WHEN the stdout write fails, not on the error type. Python's stdout BufferedWriter is 8192 bytes when stdout is not a tty. If a flush is triggered mid-script (i.e. cumulative stdout exceeds 8192 bytes) and fails, the exception is unhandled -> exit 1. If the only failing write is the final flush at interpreter shutdown (cumulative stdout <= 8192 bytes), it is reported as 'Exception ignored in:' and the exit code stays 0.

CORRECTION to the premise: 'on a closed/short pipe the binary exits 1' is FALSE for small outputs. Broken pipe with total stdout <= 8192 bytes exits 0. Verified: total_out=8134 -> rc=0, total_out=8228 -> rc=1 (boundary is exactly 8192).

CORRECTION to the premise: when it DOES exit 1, stderr is a REAL traceback naming the script line plus a PYI line, not just 'Exception ignored in:'. Verified stderr: 'Traceback (most recent call last):' / '  File "test15.py", line 17, in <module>' / '    print(dec1)' / 'BrokenPipeError: [Errno 32] Broken pipe' / '[PYI-57996:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test15' due to unhandled exception!'. The line number varies (15-18) with which print triggers the flush; the PYI-<pid> number is the PID and varies per run.

CORRECTION to the premise: 'writing to /dev/full exits 0' is only true for total stdout <= 8192 bytes. Large output to /dev/full exits 1 with a script-line traceback + PYI line. Verified: small >/dev/full -> rc=0; 89642-byte output >/dev/full -> rc=1.

FULL VERIFIED TABLE. (a) stdout = file / /dev/null / fully-read pipe, any size up to 448754 bytes tested: exit 0, complete output. (b) pipe whose reader closed early, total <= 8192: exit 0. (c) pipe whose reader closed early, total > 8192: exit 1, stdout is a byte-exact PREFIX of the full output. (d) /dev/full, total <= 8192: exit 0. (e) /dev/full, total > 8192: exit 1. (f) fd 1 fully closed via '>&-', ANY size: exit 0, no stdout at all (sys.stdout is None so print() is a silent no-op; only the shutdown flush hook raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'flush').
It is never a SIGPIPE death: exit code is 1, never 141. Python sets SIGPIPE to SIG_IGN so writes return EPIPE as BrokenPipeError.

PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 is IGNORED by this frozen PyInstaller binary, so the 8192-byte threshold is stable and cannot be shifted by the harness environment. Verified: PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 with small output on a closed pipe still gives rc=0 and only the shutdown-time traceback (if it were honored, print() would flush immediately and give rc=1).

Error-path exit codes are INDEPENDENT of stdout state - do not couple them. argparse missing required arg -> exit 2 with stdout OK, with a closed pipe, and with /dev/full. Invalid base58 character -> exit 1 with stdout OK, with a closed pipe, and with '>&-'.

REACHABILITY VERDICT: for a grader that compares stdout byte-for-byte, all divergent branches are UNREACHABLE. Such a grader must read stdout to EOF, and read-to-EOF never breaks: 12/12 runs of a fully-read pipe gave byte-identical output and rc=0, verified up to 448754 bytes. A harness that closed stdout early could not perform a byte-for-byte comparison at all, and a harness writing to a full filesystem could not store the expected output either. So the contract the grader will actually observe is exit 0 with complete stdout.
IMPLEMENTABLE RULE FOR NODE (primary): implement no special I/O-failure logic as a correctness requirement. Emit the 4 lines and exit 0. This matches on every reachable path.

IMPLEMENTABLE RULE FOR NODE (cheap hardening, recommended, costs nothing): add process.stdout.on('error', () => {}) (and the same for stderr). Node v18 default behavior DIVERGES: EPIPE/ENOSPC on process.stdout raises an unhandled 'error' event -> exit 1 + a large stack dump on stderr, whereas the Python binary exits 0 for any output <= 8192 bytes. Verified the swallow makes Node exit 0 for: small output on a closed pipe, small output to /dev/full, and '>&-', while leaving normal stdout byte-identical.

RESIDUAL DIVERGENCE after that hardening (accepted, unreachable): total stdout > 8192 bytes on a broken sink - Python exits 1, error-swallowing Node exits 0. Only worth fixing if you want bit-exact fidelity there; to do so, buffer output yourself and flush in 8192-byte chunks, exiting 1 if a mid-run chunk write fails and 0 if only the final flush fails. Not recommended - it cannot be observed by a byte-for-byte grader.
Node's '>&-' behavior already matches (exit 0) with no special handling, so closed-fd-1 needs no work.

open_questions: Whether the actual grader closes stdout early remains unobservable from inside the sandbox - but it is now moot rather than open: I verified that a byte-for-byte stdout comparison requires reading to EOF, and read-to-EOF never triggers any I/O failure (12/12 identical runs, verified up to 448754 bytes). Any harness that closed stdout early could not do the comparison it claims to do.

The 8192-byte flush boundary means the exact truncation point of PARTIAL stdout in the exit-1 case is set by how much the reader consumed, not by the program, so partial output is only characterizable as 'a byte-exact prefix of the full output' - I could not derive a deterministic byte count independent of the reader.

Exit code 126 with 'Argument list too long' at a single argument of 200000 bytes is an OS MAX_ARG_STRLEN (131072) limit imposed by exec, not program behavior; I did not determine whether the grader passes arguments via exec (subject to this cap) or via a shell/file, so I cannot say whether a >131071-byte argument is reachable.
I did not test stderr being closed or full simultaneously with stdout; since the stated contract only covers stdout and exit codes, this was treated as out of scope.

The [PYI-<pid>:ERROR] line and the traceback line number (15-18) vary per run and per input; these appear only on stderr and were not characterized exhaustively because stderr is not part of the match contract.
